---
title: "Reverse-KL intrinsic reward for prior sampling"
description: "An alternative intrinsic-reward formulation that optimizes the behavioral sampling policy by minimizing reverse KL on latent marginals."
---

::: {#key-ideas .callout-note title="Key ideas"}
- As an alternative to the trajectory-level vanilla BPO formulation in the
  [computational model of aesthetics](computational-aesthetics.qmd), the
  intrinsic policy can be trained via reinforcement learning with a step-wise
  intrinsic reward defined over policy-induced latent marginals.
- Maximizing the expected intrinsic reward under the intrinsic policy minimizes
  reverse KL divergence from its latent marginal to the single-sample
  variance-optimal importance proposal for the perceptual prior gradient, though
  reverse KL alone does not enforce support coverage or guarantee lower variance
  under restricted policy classes.
- Because the ratio of extrinsic to intrinsic latent marginals is unknown, this
  approach requires estimating that density ratio—for instance via
  least-squares importance fitting with running feature averages from extrinsic
  trajectories—and estimation error affects both the reward and the prior
  update.
:::

## Relation to the parent model

In the [computational model of aesthetics](computational-aesthetics.qmd), the
extrinsic policy $\pi_e$ optimizes task return and defines the latent
distribution that the perceptual prior $R_\theta$ should predict, while the
intrinsic policy $\pi_i$ collects samples to estimate the prior gradient. The
parent page's primary model fits $\pi_i$ with trajectory-level vanilla
[behavioral policy optimization (BPO)](behavioral-policy-optimization.qmd)
[@papini2024], minimizing forward KL over full trajectories via weighted
cross-entropy with known action-probability ratios.

This page develops an alternative that operates on single-step latent marginals
$p_\pi(z)$ instead of full trajectories and trains $\pi_i$ with an explicit
step-wise intrinsic reward $r_I(z)$.

## Reverse-KL intrinsic reward

For either policy $\pi \in \{\pi_e,\pi_i\}$, let $p_\pi(z)$ be the marginal
distribution of a latent sampled along a trajectory (for example, running $\pi$
for a fixed horizon under the same initial conditions and sampling one step
uniformly). Hold $\pi_e$, the fixed encoder $F$, and the current prior
parameters $\theta$ constant while comparing intrinsic policies.

The target prior loss and single-latent gradient are

$$
  L(\theta)=\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_e}}[-\log R_\theta(Z)],\qquad
  g_\theta(z)=\nabla_\theta[-\log R_\theta(z)].
$$

Given a latent drawn along an intrinsic trajectory, the importance-weighted
gradient estimate is

$$
  \widehat g(Z)=w(Z)g_\theta(Z),\qquad
  w(z)=\frac{p_{\pi_e}(z)}{p_{\pi_i}(z)},
$$

where the denominator measures how frequently $\pi_i$ encounters $z$. Whenever
$p_{\pi_i}(z) > 0$ wherever $p_{\pi_e}(z)g_\theta(z) \ne 0$, the estimate is
unbiased: $\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_i}}[\widehat g(Z)] = \nabla_\theta L(\theta)$.
Assuming $0 < C_\theta < \infty$ and finite second moments, the unrestricted
proposal minimizing the sum of component variances is [@alain2016, Theorem 1]

$$
  q_\theta^*(z)=\frac{p_{\pi_e}(z)\|g_\theta(z)\|_2}{C_\theta},\qquad
  C_\theta=\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_e}}\|g_\theta(Z)\|_2,
$$

which samples latents with larger prior-gradient norms more often relative to
their frequency under $\pi_e$.

Whereas vanilla BPO minimizes forward KL from the optimal proposal to the
behavioral distribution, reversing the arguments places the expectation under
the policy collecting the samples. Assigning each latent on an intrinsic
trajectory the reward

$$
  r_I(z)=\log\|g_\theta(z)\|_2
       +\log\frac{p_{\pi_e}(z)}{p_{\pi_i}(z)}
$$

yields an expected trajectory average of

$$
  \mathbb E_{p_{\pi_i}}[r_I(Z)]
  =\log C_\theta-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\pi_i}\Vert q_\theta^*),
$$

so maximizing expected intrinsic reward minimizes reverse KL.

Three limitations follow. First, reverse KL does not enforce support coverage: a
policy can earn finite expected reward while never visiting regions where
$p_{\pi_e}(z)g_\theta(z) \ne 0$, leaving the prior-gradient estimate biased, so
support coverage must be maintained separately. Second, although a policy that
can realize $q_\theta^*$ attains the single-sample variance optimum, within a
restricted policy class a smaller reverse KL need not imply lower gradient
variance. Third, this single-step criterion does not account for correlations
across successive prior updates or the nonstationarity of $r_I(z)$ as $\theta$
and the marginal ratio change during training.

## Ratio estimation with running feature averages {#sec-feature-ema}

Because $p_{\pi_e}(z)$ and $p_{\pi_i}(z)$ are unknown, evaluating both $r_I(z)$
and $\widehat g(z)$ requires estimating their density ratio $w(z)$. Rather than
estimating the two marginals separately, least-squares importance fitting
[@kanamori2009, sec. 2.2] targets the ratio directly by minimizing

$$
  \mathcal L(w)=\tfrac12\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_i}}[w(Z)^2]
                   -\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_e}}[w(Z)].
$$

When $p_{\pi_i}$ covers the support of $p_{\pi_e}$ and the true ratio
$w^*(Z) = p_{\pi_e}(Z)/p_{\pi_i}(Z)$ has finite second moment under $p_{\pi_i}$,
$\mathcal L(w)$ differs from
$\tfrac12\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_i}}[(w(Z) - w^*(Z))^2]$ only by an additive constant.

With a linear feature model $w_\eta(z)=\eta^\top f(z)$, we can maintain an
exponential moving average $m_e$ of the fixed features $f(z)$ **from extrinsic
trajectories only**. Then $\eta^\top m_e$ approximates the second expectation
while intrinsic trajectory samples supply the first. The choice of features
determines which distributional differences the estimator can resolve: one-hot
features track category frequencies, whereas the mean of a continuous latent
cannot distinguish distributions that share a mean but differ in their tails.

On each intrinsic trajectory, the pre-update estimate $w_\eta(z)$ enters in two
places: $\log w_\eta(z)$ adds to $\log\|g_\theta(z)\|_2$ in the intrinsic
reward, and $w_\eta(z)$ scales $g_\theta(z)$ in the prior update. Because the
reward takes logarithms, both weights and gradient norms must stay positive;
enforcing positivity or flooring small estimates introduces approximation error,
and limited features, correlated samples, or drift in $\pi_e$ and $\pi_i$ all
degrade both the reward signal and the prior-gradient estimate.
